title: People and Family
description: The family words you will be asked about in the first five minutes of any conversation, and the little endings -i and -ak/-ik that turn 'mother' into 'my mother' and 'your mother'.
approach: Here-and-now with a family tree: every word is heard while a figure on the tree lights up; the possessive endings are taught by moving a 'my' and 'your' token onto the tree.
unlock_condition: ≥10/13 on the family-tree tap quiz and one recorded line about your own family
can_do: Name the members of a family

grammar.title: -i, -ak, -ik: my and your, stuck on the end
grammar.explanation: Arabic does not have a separate word for 'my' or 'your'. You add an ending to the noun: -i means my (بيتي my house, أختي my sister), -ak means your when talking to a man (بيتك, أختك), and -ik when talking to a woman (in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the Emirates this -ik becomes -ich, spelled ـج: أختج). Two family words end in a vowel and take a y instead: أبوي my father, أخوي my brother. You already did this in اسمي and اسمك without noticing.

examples.english: My mother and father are at home

culture.title: How is the family? — the question that wants no answer
culture.note: After شلونك the next question is almost always شلون الأهل؟ or شخبار الأهل؟ — how is the family — and the expected answer is بخير الحمد لله, not news. Asking a man about his children, parents and brothers is warm and normal; asking a man about his wife by name is not, so ask about الأهل or البيت instead. Between women the same questions are asked freely. Whether you are married and have children will be asked early and directly — it is interest, not intrusion.

culture.title: Abu and Umm: called by your child's name
culture.note: Once a couple has a son, everyone calls them أبو and أم + his name — أبو فهد, أم فهد — and in the Gulf أبو shortens to بو in address: يا بو فهد. It is respectful and affectionate at the same time, so it is the safe way to address a peer or an elder whose son you know. Older men are also addressed as عمي (my uncle) and older women as خالتي (my aunt) by anyone younger, family or not.

phrases.english: How are you, uncle? (to any older man)

vocabulary.teaching_note: With the ending: أمي ummi (my mother). Calling to her, Gulf children say يمّه yumma — you will hear it constantly in family vlogs. ماما is also universal at home. Also the first half of the kunya أم فهد.
vocabulary.image_scene: A mother in a colourful house dress holding a toddler on her hip in a bright kitchen.

example.english: My mother is in the kitchen

vocabulary.video_hint: Children calling يمّه; a vlogger introducing أمي on camera.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Gulf form ends in a vowel, so 'my father' is أبوي abuuy and 'your father' أبوك abuuk. The same word starts every kunya: أبو محمد. At home children say بابا or يبه yuba. The MSA أب is never used in speech.
vocabulary.image_scene: A father in a white thobe and ghutra sitting cross-legged with a child on his knee.

example.english: My father is in the majlis

vocabulary.video_hint: A father addressed as يبه or بابا; anyone called أبو / بو + name.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Like أبو it grows a vowel before the ending: أخوي akhuuy (my brother), أخوك akhuuk (your brother). يا أخوي — brother — is also the everyday friendly address to any man, related or not. Plural إخوان.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two young men with matching features standing shoulder to shoulder, one arm over the other's shoulder.
vocabulary.video_hint: Sibling introductions in family vlogs; يا أخوي between friends.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Regular: أختي ukhti, أختك ukhtak / ukhtik. Plural خوات khawaat, a very Gulf form. يا أختي is the polite way to address a woman you do not know.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two young women in abayas laughing together on a sofa, clearly sisters.

example.english: My sister is a student at university

vocabulary.video_hint: A vlogger mentioning أختي; يا أختي to a woman in a shop.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Pronounced ibin in the Gulf. In everyday speech most people say ولدي (my boy) for 'my son', so you will hear ابن mostly in ابني and in phrases like ابن عمي (my cousin). Learn both.
vocabulary.image_scene: A father with his hand on the shoulder of a teenage boy in a thobe, both smiling at the camera.
vocabulary.video_hint: Parents introducing a son; ابن عم / ابن خال for cousins.

vocabulary.teaching_note: بنتي is my daughter. The same word means 'girl' in general, so context decides. Plural بنات. Also in بنت عمي (my cousin, f) and the polite يا بنت الناس.
vocabulary.image_scene: A mother brushing the hair of a small girl in a party dress.
vocabulary.video_hint: Parents naming a daughter; بناتي in family vlogs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The word people actually use: أهلي my family, شلون أهلك؟ how is your family. عائلة (family as a unit) exists but is more formal. Also means 'the people of' a place: أهل الكويت.
vocabulary.image_scene: An extended family of three generations seated together on floor cushions around a large tray.
vocabulary.video_hint: Family gatherings; the greeting شخبار الأهل.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Said ṣidiig in the Gulf (ق = g). صديقي my friend, صديقتي my friend (f). For your group of friends Gulf speakers say ربع rabʿ — ربعي, 'my gang' — and Kuwaitis also say رفيج. Between men, أخوي and يا أخوي are just as common.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two young men in thobes sharing a laugh over tea glasses at a café table.
vocabulary.video_hint: Friends introduced on camera; ربعي in outing and camping vlogs.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A doubled j: rajjaal. In Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the Emirates the ج becomes y — ريّال rayyaal — and that is how they write it too. Plural رجاجيل / رياييل. The MSA رجل is not used.
vocabulary.image_scene: A middle-aged man in a white thobe and red-checked shemagh standing in a doorway.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone pointing out a man; listen for rajjaal vs rayyaal to place the speaker.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The everyday Gulf word for woman, also used by a man for his wife (حرمتي). Plural حريم. مرة is a blunter alternative. Avoid the MSA امرأة, which nobody says. Starts with the deep ح.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman in a black abaya and shayla carrying shopping bags in a mall.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone describing a woman; حريم for the women's side of a gathering.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Boy, and by extension son (ولدي). Plural أولاد or the very Gulf عيال (kids), which you heard in عندك عيال؟. Also a friendly address to a younger man: يا ولد.
vocabulary.image_scene: A boy of about eight in a small white thobe kicking a football in a yard.

example.english: The boy is in the street

vocabulary.video_hint: Children playing; a parent calling a son.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Gulf word for a girl or young woman, especially in Kuwait, Bahrain and the Emirates; بنوتة is the affectionate Saudi form and بنت works everywhere. Choosing بنية here keeps 'girl' and 'daughter' apart on the flashcards.
vocabulary.image_scene: A girl of about eight in a bright dress holding a balloon at a park.
vocabulary.video_hint: Children in family vlogs; بنية / بنوتة said of a small girl.

vocabulary.teaching_note: جدتي my grandmother. Kuwait and the Emirates say يدّة yadda (ج → y) and this shows the split clearly. Grandmothers are the centre of Friday lunch, so the word comes up every week.
vocabulary.image_scene: An elderly woman in a headscarf seated on cushions, pouring tea for grandchildren.
vocabulary.video_hint: Visits to a grandmother; زيارة جدتي vlogs.

dialogue.speaker: Khalid

dialogue.speaker: Fahad

dialogue.transliteration: hala wallah, tsharrafna. ana fahad, ṣidiig khaalid

dialogue.transliteration: hala fiik ya bu saʿuud. abuuy w-ummi bil-majlis

sound_spotlight.explanation: One letter, two voices. Saudis say j; Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the Emirates say y in inherited words like جدة and رجال. The app plays both. Listen for it and you can place a speaker in seconds; the meaning never changes.
The feminine your ending is -ik in Saudi and -ich further up the Gulf. You are not asked to say the ch yet — only to recognise أختج and بنتج as the same word as أختك and بنتك.
Unlike Cairo or Beirut, the Gulf keeps the th sounds: ث as in 'think', ذ as in 'this'. هذا has the second one. Next lesson's numbers are full of the first.

lesson_sequence.detail: A family tree drawn on a majlis wall. One line of English: today you name the people around you and say whose they are. Tap يلّا.
Thirteen cards; as each word plays, the matching figure on the family tree lights up. Arabic large, English small. Tap any figure to hear its word again.
A token labelled -i and one labelled -ak/-ik are dragged onto tree figures; the app says the suffixed form (أمي, أختك). Then the learner hears a suffixed form and drags the right token.
Audio only: أخوي / أخوك / أختي / أختك; the learner taps 'mine' or 'yours' and the gender of the listener when it is -ik/-ich.
The learner records one line about their own family from a menu: أمي وأبوي في …, عندي أخ / أخت. Speech check marks the ending.
The dialogue plays with figures highlighted; then thirteen tap items on the tree with audio only.
Counter rolls to 65. Nudge: next time someone asks شلون الأهل؟ answer بخير الحمد لله without thinking.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Open your phone's family photos and name each person out loud: أمي، أبوي، أخوي، أختي.
real_world_prompts.context: Lesson-complete screen. Here-and-now practice with the learner's own people.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Ask an Arabic-speaking friend شلون الأهل؟ today. Expect بخير الحمد لله — and give the same when it comes back.
real_world_prompts.context: Next-day notification. The most common second question in any Gulf conversation.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Tell your tutor about three people in your family in three short sentences: أخوي طالب. أمي من …. أبوي بالبيت.
real_world_prompts.context: Before a tutor session. Recycles Lesson 4 sentence shape with Lesson 5 words.

video_needs.scene: Family vlogs where members are introduced or called by name: a mother naming her children, a vlogger saying هذا أخوي, children shouting يمّه — the person visible when the word is said.
